items.title: [9M2PJU] Velocity OSINT Tracker: Self-Hosted Flight, Ship and Satellite Replay Without API Keys
items.content_html:
Velocity (AndrewCTF/velocity, v1.3.1) is a self-hosted, AGPL-3.0 flight, vessel, satellite, and hazard console that records live ADS-B, AIS, CelesTrak SGP4, and GPS jamming feeds onto local TimescaleDB or SQLite storage with 1x to 3600x replay, local readsb/tar1090 ingest, an ESP32 /api/overhead endpoint, and a 94-tool MCP server without requiring API keys.

The post Velocity OSINT Tracker: Self-Hosted Flight, Ship and Satellite Replay Without API Keys appeared on HamRadio.my - Amateur Radio, Tech Insights and Reviews by 9M2PJU.

items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] Bambu Lab P3C is here: Tool changer, now standard
items.content_html:
Surely, they could have made many other decisions to reduce the price, but delivering it with 2 nozzles, would not really make it competitive to the U1 or any other tool changer.

And the P3C is an answer to the U1.

It swaps tools (and therefore materials) in less than 4 seconds, but people complain about the initial loading time of the filament. It is still a hobby machine.

When you know on forehand that you constantly need to load different materials, you can always go for the U1 or another machine from the competition if you think it better. Don’t underestimate all the other hassle that comes with those machines.

It’s an entry tool changer machine with a competitive price.

And it’s pretty hard to build a one-size-fits-all solution in 3D Printing. I bet the engineers and marketers will have had many discussions over this topic for sure.

And maybe in the near future, an Automatic loading AMS will be released.

items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] Loud Clattering/Clicking,
items.content_html:
Hello,

This is the response from Bambu Lab Support.

Dear Customer,

Thank you for your reply.

We’ve reviewed your video, and there’s nothing obviously abnormal during the manual movement. The sound isn’t coming from the idler pulley.

The sound you hear while printing is most likely caused by the toolhead starting and stopping quickly over short distances, which produces a mechanical sound as the motion absorbs the impact. This is normal and won’t affect the printer’s performance.

Because the H3C prints with higher speed and acceleration than our other models, this sound tends to be more noticeable on the H3C.

If the sound bothers you and you’d like to reduce it, there are two things you can try: 1. Turn on Silent Mode. You can switch it on directly in “Settings” on the printer’s screen, and it can effectively reduce operating noise. 2. Adjust the slicer settings. In your slicer (such as Bambu Studio), lower the maximum acceleration a little, then re-slice and print again. This can also noticeably reduce the sound.

If you still have any issues after making these adjustments, please don’t hesitate to contact us.

Best regards,
Bambu Lab Customer Support

The support team’s response isn’t entirely satisfactory, but it makes sense. The print quality is good. The only real downside: Compared to the H2C, it’s significantly louder.

items.title: [lxer.com] CachyOS adds Easy Anti-Cheat v2 support; Fortnite expected first
items.content_html: The November release of CachyOS, an Arch-based distribution, adds support for Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2, a game-protection system that checks a computer’s boot setup before allowing a game to start. Heise reported that no game was using the Linux v2 system yet and that Fortnite is expected to be the first. CachyOS supplies a separate signed kernel and boot option for EAC-protected games, while the standard boot entries remain available. Enabling the EAC option requires Secure Boot, a trusted signing key, TPM 2.0, an enabled IOMMU and kernel lockdown. The release also includes a redesigned package installer and a recovery environment for Btrfs snapshots.

Large Prints: Say Goodbye to Warping! Community Contributions
[翘边_首图_en] How often does this situation happen to you? The printer has printed half of the model. The model’s bottom lifts off the print bed - warping. We need to trash the whole model. Large prints tend to warp, like furniture parts. When we make 3D-printed tools and add more wall layers to make them stronger, they sometimes warp. You can see how warping looks and where it occurs in the image below. [image] In our first Bambu Lab flagstore, you can see and experience the massive CyberBr…

Personally, if a brim or mouse ears aren’t enough to reliably hold the print down, it’s usually back to the design for me. Even with glue as adhesive (eg. on Engineering plate), a bad warp may lift the plate instead (which can be hard to notice). And I don’t like glue anyway.

Cheers,
-Max

items.title: [andi@undisclosed.example.com andi] Still Alive revived
items.content_html:
Still Alive revived

Back in 2008, I blogged about a little homebrew game for the Nintendo DS named StillAliveDS and how much I liked the puzzle platformer.

StillAliveDS is a puzzle game inspired by Portal: The Flash Version, which is a 2D remake of Portal, developed by Valve Corporation.

Portal consists primarily of a series of puzzles that must be solved by teleporting the character and other simple objects using a Portal Gun. The unusual physics allowed by the Portal Gun are the emphasis of Portal.

A few weeks ago, I used my website's random button and landed on exactly that post. I wondered whatever became of the game. To my surprise, I learned that its developer, “t4ils,” had made a web version and released it under the AGPL.

Unfortunately, the website was no longer available, but the Wayback Machine still had parts of it. There was enough to recover all the client-side code.

It still worked in modern browsers, but it used an ancient version of jQuery, and the tiny DS-resolution graphics weren't great on modern systems.

So I spent quite some time “reviving” the game with the help of Claude. I wanted to keep the gameplay, look, and feel as close to the original as possible while thoroughly modernizing the game.

To nobody's surprise, Claude was able to make the game run again in no time. Refactoring the code and graphics into a modern architecture, on the other hand, took a lot of babysitting and reviewing. The current architecture is the result of many, many iterations.

Tiles and background graphics had to be redrawn from scratch while staying close to the original. Though I made the creative decision to drop a few “jokes” from the background images that I felt were a bit out of date – I don't think anyone misses jokes about Michael Jackson's looks in 2026.

Since the licensing of the original audio was a bit unclear, I decided to replace the sound effects and also extend them to cover more actions. Finding the right effects took quite a while – Claude helped me by building a “sound lab” where I could test and compare sound effects from different free sources until I found what I needed.

Even though the game now uses a modern ES module structure and web components for the UI, I decided not to use a bundler. Instead, it relies on modern browsers' module-loading support. A custom loader loads all assets into RAM once. This way, there are no external dependencies (neither libraries nor build tools), and the game can be restored from the Wayback Machine, just like the original could.

The game can be played right in your browser: Still Alive revived.

Currently, only mouse and keyboard are supported. If I feel like it, I might add controller support someday. I don't know if or how it could ever be made to support touch controls.
